notes.text: For more than 6, sear the steak in two batches so the pan stays hot. Keep the first batch resting on the board while the second cooks.

move.title: A green sauce, chopped by hand
move.body: Fine chopping means cutting herbs and garlic into tiny, even bits. Today you'll chop parsley and garlic for chimichurri, a bright Argentine sauce, then sear a steak in a hot pan and spoon the sauce over the slices.

callback.body: In fajitas you left the chicken alone in a hot pan until a brown crust formed and it let go by itself. Steak works the same way. Don't poke it, and wait for the crust.

why.title: Keep the tip down
why.body: Rest the tip of the knife on the board and lift only the handle, up and down, like a seesaw. Your other hand presses flat on top of the blade, away from the edge. The tip never leaves the board, so the knife can't jump.

why.title: Let the sauce sit
why.body: Salt and vinegar pull flavor out of the garlic and herbs, and the oil carries it around the bowl. Chimichurri made 15 minutes ahead tastes stronger and rounder than chimichurri made a minute ago. Make it first, and let it sit while the steak cooks.

why.title: Dry meat browns, wet meat steams
why.body: Water on the outside of the steak has to boil away before the meat can brown. Until it does, the steak just steams and turns gray. Patting it dry with paper towels lets the crust start right away.

why.title: Why the steak rests
why.body: Right out of the pan, the juice inside hot meat is moving around fast. Cut it now and the juice runs out onto the board. Five minutes of rest lets it settle, so it stays in the steak.

why.title: Across the grain
why.body: Steak is made of long, stringy fibers, all lying the same way. Slice along them and each piece is a bundle of long strings to chew through. Slice across them and every piece has short fibers that come apart easily.

wrong.sign: The steak is gray, not brown
wrong.fix: The pan wasn't hot enough, or the steak was wet. Leave it on a little longer without moving it. Next time, pat it dry and wait for the oil to shimmer.
They were cut along the grain. Turn the steak a quarter turn and cut the rest the other way. Cutting thinner helps too.
Stir in a spoonful more olive oil and let it sit a few more minutes.

wrong.sign: There are big chunks of garlic
wrong.fix: Scoop them out, rock the knife over them a few more times, and stir them back in.

quiz.q: Why do you pat the steak dry before it goes in the pan?
choices: So it browns instead of steaming
quiz.explain: Water has to boil off before meat can brown. Dry meat starts browning right away.

quiz.q: Which way do you slice the cooked steak?
choices: Along the lines in the meat
Across the lines in the meat
quiz.explain: Slicing across the grain makes short fibers, so each bite is tender.

steps.text: Rinse the parsley in the colander and roll it up in the kitchen towel to pat it dry. Pull the leaves off the thick stems and push them into a tight pile on the cutting board.
steps.tip: Dry leaves chop into neat bits. Wet ones turn to mush.

steps.text: Chop the parsley fine: rest the tip of the knife on the board, press your other hand flat on top of the blade, and rock the handle up and down over the pile. Scrape it back together and go over it again until the bits are small. Put it in the small bowl.
steps.look: Fluffy green bits about the size of a grain of rice.

steps.text: Peel the garlic. Mince it: chop it, then rock the knife over it until the bits are tiny. Add it to the bowl.
steps.tip: Press each clove under the flat of the knife first. The skin cracks and peels right off.

steps.text: Add the oregano, the vinegar, the olive oil, {qty:salt} salt, and the chili flakes if you're using them. Stir with the fork and set the sauce aside.
Lay the steak on the plate and pat it dry on both sides with paper towels. Sprinkle both sides with the steak's salt and the pepper, and press them on with your hand.
Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw steak or its package touched.
Heat the vegetable oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay the steak in the pan, laying it down away from you. Put the tongs in the sink, and don't use them again for cooked food.
steps.tip: It should sizzle loudly the second it touches. If it doesn't, the pan needs more heat next time.

steps.text: Wash your hands, and put the raw-steak plate in the sink. From here on, use the clean spatula.
Leave the steak alone while the bottom sears. Don't poke it or move it.
steps.look: A deep brown crust, and it lets go of the pan when you nudge it.

steps.text: Flip the steak with the spatula and sear the other side.
steps.tip: Lift it and flip it away from you, so any spatter goes the other way.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the side of the steak, into the thickest part. It needs to read at least 145°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute on each side and check again.
Turn off the stove. Move the steak to the cutting board with the spatula and let it rest.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.

steps.text: Look for the thin lines running along the steak. Turn the steak so they run left to right, and slice it thin, across the grain.
steps.look: Each slice shows short little lines across its cut face, not long strings.

steps.text: Lay the slices on a plate, stir the chimichurri, and spoon it over the top.
steps.tip: Pour any juice from the cutting board over the steak too. It's full of flavor.
